concepts.name: Defining mindfulness
concepts.summary: Can state that mindfulness is paying attention to present experience on purpose and without judgment.

concepts.name: Posture and setup
concepts.summary: Can explain how an alert, comfortable posture and quiet setting support practice.

concepts.name: Breath as anchor
concepts.summary: Understands why the breath serves as a neutral, always-available object for attention.

concepts.name: Noticing wandering mind
concepts.summary: Understands that the mind wandering is normal and that noticing it is the core moment of practice.

concepts.name: Gentle return of attention
concepts.summary: Can describe returning attention kindly without self-criticism each time it drifts.

concepts.name: Short daily sessions
concepts.summary: Can recall that short, regular sessions of a few minutes are enough to begin.

misconceptions.text: Meditation means emptying the mind of all thoughts.
If my mind wanders, I am failing at meditation.
You must sit cross-legged on the floor to meditate properly.

concepts.name: Counting and labeling breaths
concepts.summary: Can apply counting or silent labeling to stabilise attention during a sitting.

concepts.name: Body scan sequence
concepts.summary: Can guide attention systematically through body regions, noticing sensations without trying to change them.

concepts.name: Distinguishing sensation from story
concepts.summary: Can separate raw physical sensations from thoughts and interpretations about them.

concepts.name: Loving-kindness phrases
concepts.summary: Can practise silently repeating kind phrases toward self and then others.

concepts.name: Handling sleepiness and restlessness
concepts.summary: Can apply simple adjustments such as posture, eyes open or shorter sits when drowsy or restless.

concepts.name: Informal mindfulness
concepts.summary: Can bring mindful attention to routine activities like eating or walking.

misconceptions.text: The body scan is a relaxation technique meant to make you feel calm every time.
Loving-kindness only works if you genuinely feel warmth during the phrases.
Mindfulness only happens during formal sitting sessions.

concepts.name: Open monitoring practice
concepts.summary: Can sustain receptive awareness of whatever arises without fixating on a single object.

concepts.name: Focused versus open attention
concepts.summary: Can compare the two meditation styles and choose one to fit a goal or state of mind.

concepts.name: Building a daily routine
concepts.summary: Can design a realistic routine using fixed time, place and cues to sustain practice.

concepts.name: Equanimity and non-striving
concepts.summary: Can practise meeting pleasant, unpleasant and neutral experience with even-minded acceptance.

concepts.name: Working with difficult emotions
concepts.summary: Can analyse an arising emotion and respond with recognising, allowing and investigating rather than suppressing or reacting.

concepts.name: Stress response and pausing
concepts.summary: Can analyse how stress reactions unfold and use a brief mindful pause to interrupt them.

concepts.name: Practice journaling and review
concepts.summary: Can examine practice notes to identify patterns, obstacles and progress.

misconceptions.text: Mindfulness is meant to eliminate stress and unpleasant emotions.
Open monitoring is just daydreaming with no structure.
Acceptance means passively putting up with everything and not acting.

concepts.name: Tailoring practice to attention goals
concepts.summary: Can evaluate which practices best train sustained focus, meta-awareness or cognitive flexibility and adapt a program accordingly.

concepts.name: Meta-awareness and decentering
concepts.summary: Can analyse thoughts as mental events rather than facts and shift into an observing stance.

concepts.name: Practice during daily demands
concepts.summary: Can judge where and how to apply mindful techniques to meetings, workload and digital distraction.

concepts.name: Compassion and self-compassion
concepts.summary: Can analyse self-criticism patterns and apply compassion practices to relate to them differently.

concepts.name: Recognising meditation difficulties
concepts.summary: Can evaluate when practice is causing distress such as dissociation or rumination and modify or seek support.

concepts.name: Appraising evidence for mindfulness
concepts.summary: Can critically appraise claims about mindfulness benefits, noting effect sizes, controls and limits of studies.

misconceptions.text: Meditation is always safe and beneficial for everyone, with no possible downsides.
Self-compassion is just self-indulgence that lowers motivation.
Research has proven mindfulness works equally well as a treatment for all conditions.

concepts.name: Designing personalised practice programs
concepts.summary: Can create a tailored, progressive practice plan integrating focus, open monitoring, body-based and compassion practices for an individual's needs.

concepts.name: Guiding others in meditation
concepts.summary: Can create and deliver clear guided instructions with appropriate pacing, language and inquiry.

concepts.name: Contemplative traditions and secular adaptation
concepts.summary: Can evaluate how secular programs differ from and draw on traditional contemplative frameworks.

concepts.name: Trauma-sensitive adaptation
concepts.summary: Can design practice and instruction choices that offer safety, choice and alternatives to internal focus for vulnerable participants.

concepts.name: Evaluating practice outcomes
concepts.summary: Can assess the effects of practice using sound criteria, self-report limits and behavioural indicators.

concepts.name: Integrating insight into conduct
concepts.summary: Can judge how awareness, ethics and compassion translate into skilful action and avoid spiritual bypassing.

misconceptions.text: A single standard technique suits every person and context.
Secular mindfulness programs are identical to traditional Buddhist practice.
Feeling calm and detached is proof that practice is working and insight has been gained.
